claims.text: A machine-learned force field combined with the Green–Kubo formalism can predict phonon thermal conductivity in single-phase high-entropy alloys.
The proposed approach will be more accurate than standard DFT-based or empirical methods.
The proposed approach works better because it captures force-constant fluctuations caused by atomic-scale chemical disorder.
Single-phase HEAs generally exhibit severe lattice distortion and random atomic arrangements.
The approach is applicable to thermal-insulation HEAs over approximately 300–700 K.
The approach is limited to alloys that remain single-phase and lack strong magnetic interactions or comparable complexities.
High-entropy chemical mixing produces local chemical disorder and atomic-level force-constant fluctuations.
Force-constant fluctuations in a disordered HEA scatter and attenuate phonons.
Severe lattice distortion strongly scatters heat-carrying phonons and thereby lowers lattice thermal conductivity.
Accurately modeling dynamic interatomic interactions and force fluctuations improves the representation of phonon scattering and damping.
A more detailed representation of phonon damping produces more reliable predictions of low lattice thermal conductivity.
The proposed method will predict lower thermal-conductivity values that agree better with experiment.
The proposed method will improve predictive accuracy by roughly 10–20% relative to traditional DFT-based or empirical models.
Traditional predictive models do not fully account for enhanced phonon scattering from complex force-constant fluctuations in disordered HEAs.
Predictions may fail for multiphase alloys, strongly magnetic systems, or extremely inhomogeneous systems.
Predictive improvement depends on the quality and representativeness of the machine-learned force field's training data.
The method's performance at temperature extremes has not been fully validated.
The benchmark will compare simulated lattice thermal conductivity with independent experimental thermal-conductivity and phonon-attenuation measurements across multiple single-phase HEAs.
The hypothesis is falsified if predicted conductivities differ from experiment by more than 20% across the sample set or if the method fails to reproduce the trend with increasing chemical disorder.
